question: Move the AED at The Cathedral School (Cathedral of St. John the Divine) into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: The Cathedral School (Cathedral of St. John the Divine) (School, ZIP 10025) has a registered AED at "Undercroft, Crypt Gym; Third Floor, Gym; Security; First Floor, Desk".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.19 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 7 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 11 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists FDNY Engine 47, a fire station normally staffed around the clock, 106 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving this AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet directly addresses a documented gap. The school's current indoor placement is unreachable during 113 of 168 weekly hours during the school year and entirely inaccessible in summer [E3]. Last year, the area experienced 1.19 cardiac-arrest calls annually when every nearby AED was closed [E4]—ranking seventh among NYC schools in this vulnerability. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. A street-wall cabinet would eliminate access barriers while the school maintains its existing device.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: Before moving this AED, we should exhaust cheaper alternatives. Yes, the area saw 1.19 calls yearly during closed hours [E4], but that's a small number—we don't know where those calls actually occurred within the ZIP [E9]. More importantly, FDNY Engine 47 sits just 106 meters away and is staffed around the clock [E8]. Installing a 24/7 AED there would solve the access problem without cabinet costs or vandalism risks [E9]. The school's current placement already reaches 55 of 168 weekly hours during the school year [E3]. Moving it outdoors may help, but we need cost estimates and vandalism data [E9] before committing resources when a fire station alternative exists.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The fire station alternative deserves serious consideration, but it doesn't eliminate the case for moving the school's AED. Engine 47's proximity is valuable, yet we cannot assume it will host a new device—that requires separate negotiation and approval. Meanwhile, the school's current AED remains inaccessible during the 1.19 annual cardiac-arrest calls that occurred when all nearby devices were closed [E4]. Moving it to a street cabinet creates immediate 24/7 availability without depending on another agency's cooperation. The skeptic rightly notes we lack cost and vandalism data [E9], but those are implementation details, not reasons to delay addressing a documented gap. Both solutions could coexist; they're not mutually exclusive.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The Advocate makes a fair point that we shouldn't wait for perfect data, but the fire station alternative is too concrete to ignore. Engine 47 is already staffed 24/7 just 106 meters away [E8]—that's a real, immediate option requiring no new cabinet infrastructure. Yes, we'd need to negotiate with FDNY [E9], but that's far cheaper and faster than installing outdoor equipment. The 1.19 annual calls during closed hours [E4] matter, yet we don't know if they'd actually be closer to the school's wall than to the fire station [E9]. We should pursue Engine 47 first. If FDNY declines, then the school cabinet becomes the fallback—not the first move.

verdict.summary: Documented gap exists (1.19 annual calls during AED closure [E4]), but moving the school's AED should follow investigation of the FDNY Engine 47 alternative 106 m away [E8] and cost/vandalism data [E9].
verdict.strongestFor: School's current placement unreachable 113/168 weekly hours [E3]; 1.19 annual calls occurred when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]; public AED shock associated with 66.5% survival versus 43.0% [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: FDNY Engine 47 already staffed 24/7 just 106 m away [E8]; unknown cabinet costs, vandalism risk, and actual call locations within ZIP [E9]; 1.19 calls is small sample without precise geographic data [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Contact FDNY Engine 47 to assess feasibility of hosting a 24/7 AED; obtain cabinet cost and vandalism data; map actual 2025 call locations against both sites.
